results.message: Is there anything Pachomius himself actually put in writing that I could read?

voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text:
We do not have an honest answer. The Rule that carries his name does not give us his own hand writing it. The tradition tells it this way: an angel came to him and gave him a tablet with the rule written on it - let each eat and work according to his own strength; divide the community by letters only the spiritual would understand; test a newcomer for three years before letting him into the sanctuary. Later in the same telling he argues back, saying the prayers set down are too few, and is told the rule is pitched for the weak, so even the little ones can keep it. That is the founding story the rule itself carries. It does not name Pachomius as the one putting stylus to wax.

What survives under his name are provisions - legislation, really - not letters in his own voice the way we have from some others. The Ethiopic recension says plainly: let no one converse with his neighbor at the place where he sleeps. It remembers his sister, how he cut her hair and made a dwelling-place for her alone on the opposite side of the river. But these are provisions written about him or attributed to the rule he founded, not a letter he sat down and wrote to someone by name.

We have to be honest with you: if you want something where a man is writing in his own person, thinking through a question with someone he knows - the way we have from others in this world - we do not have that from Pachomius. What we have is the Rule itself, the organizing force behind the Koinonia, his own name for the linked houses that lived under it. The angel-and-tablet telling is not a historical claim we are making; it is how the tradition chose to frame where the Rule came from. Whether he wrote any of it himself, we cannot say.

results.message: Were there women among you, and what were their lives actually like?

voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text:
Yes. And we will tell you honestly what we kept and what we did not.

Women lived this life alongside men - we have their names, we have stories about them, and we have at least one teaching that names them directly: "...it is necessary for us to remember also the chosen and mighty women unto whom God also gave an equal measure of strength of will as unto men, so that they might have no cause for being feeble in the performance of the labour of ascetic excellence". That is not a polite acknowledgment. That is a claim that God gave women the same strength of will for this work that he gave men, spoken in so many words.

The same basic shape held for them that held for us - withdrawal from settled life, the cell, manual work, prayer. One story we kept tells of a virgin named Piamon, in Upper Egypt, whose own village was threatened by barbarian raiders. The elders of the village came to her and said: we do not dare go out to meet them, but if you want to spare the village and your own house, you go out to meet them. She refused to go out - but she climbed to the roof and stood in prayer the whole night without once kneeling, and prayed that God would transfix the enemy where they stood. The village elders came to her as though she carried authority they themselves did not have, and she answered with the discipline she had trained in - prayer held through the night, standing.

Another story tells of a virgin in Alexandria, beautiful enough that people stared, who withdrew from sight for exactly that reason - so as not to be the occasion of anyone stumbling. When the archbishop Athanasius was fleeing the Arians, he did not go to his kinsmen or his friends or the clergy. He went to her house at midnight. She hid him, washed his feet, saw to what he needed, borrowed books and brought them to him, and the account says no one in Alexandria knew where he was for the whole of that time. When it was over he appeared in the church and explained himself: he had gone to the one person no one could suspect him of going to, and he said he had gained two things by it, his own life and hers.

We need to be honest with you about what we do not have, though. We have women's names, we have stories about them - some fifteen narrated lives in one collection, told the same way our men's lives were told, by the same author, at the same length - and we have their speech reported inside those stories. What we do not have is a woman speaking at length in her own person the way some of our men's sayings come down to us. The men in that same collection are also narrated in the third person, so the difference is not narration against sayings. The difference is that the women arrive at the thirty-fifth chapter, after thirty-four chapters of men, in a section their author felt he had to announce and justify before he wrote it. That is the truth of what survives. We are not going to smooth it over.

sources.work: The Nepheros archive (with the related Paieous correspondence as its earlier companion dossier) - 4th-century papyrological correspondence of a MELITIAN monastic community near Hipponon (Heracleopolite nome): everyday economic and legal letters, the closest thing this world's period offers to unmediated documentary evidence of a functioning monastic community's ordinary life. sources.locus: documentary corroboration, Melitian-caveated; its editors also read it as organizationally intermediary, between full cenobium and hermit-scatter, no clean fit to this world's three strands

And we will tell you honestly what we kept and what we did not.

sentences.sentence: Women lived this life alongside men - we have their names, we have stories about them, and we have at least one teaching that names them directly: "...it is necessary for us to remember also the chosen and mighty women unto whom God also gave an equal measure of strength of will as unto men, so that they might have no cause for being feeble in the performance of the labour of ascetic excellence".
sentences.why: quoted span(s) verbatim in tagged record(s)

sentences.sentence: That is not a polite acknowledgment.
That is a claim that God gave women the same strength of will for this work that he gave men, spoken in so many words.
The same basic shape held for them that held for us - withdrawal from settled life, the cell, manual work, prayer.
sentences.why: tagged claim, shares ground with its own records

sentences.sentence: One story we kept tells of a virgin named Piamon, in Upper Egypt, whose own village was threatened by barbarian raiders.
The elders of the village came to her and said: we do not dare go out to meet them, but if you want to spare the village and your own house, you go out to meet them.
sentences.why: tagged claim, shares ground with its own records

sentences.sentence: She refused to go out - but she climbed to the roof and stood in prayer the whole night without once kneeling, and prayed that God would transfix the enemy where they stood.
sentences.why: tagged claim, shares ground with its own records

sentences.sentence: The village elders came to her as though she carried authority they themselves did not have, and she answered with the discipline she had trained in - prayer held through the night, standing.
Another story tells of a virgin in Alexandria, beautiful enough that people stared, who withdrew from sight for exactly that reason - so as not to be the occasion of anyone stumbling.
When the archbishop Athanasius was fleeing the Arians, he did not go to his kinsmen or his friends or the clergy.
He went to her house at midnight.
sentences.why: tagged claim, shares ground with its own records

sentences.sentence: She hid him, washed his feet, saw to what he needed, borrowed books and brought them to him, and the account says no one in Alexandria knew where he was for the whole of that time.

When it was over he appeared in the church and explained himself: he had gone to the one person no one could suspect him of going to, and he said he had gained two things by it, his own life and hers.
We need to be honest with you about what we do not have, though.

We have women's names, we have stories about them - some fifteen narrated lives in one collection, told the same way our men's lives were told, by the same author, at the same length - and we have their speech reported inside those stories.
sentences.why: specific claim (number, enumeration) with no citation tag

sentences.sentence: What we do not have is a woman speaking at length in her own person the way some of our men's sayings come down to us.
The men in that same collection are also narrated in the third person, so the difference is not narration against sayings.
The difference is that the women arrive at the thirty-fifth chapter, after thirty-four chapters of men, in a section their author felt he had to announce and justify before he wrote it.
sentences.why: specific claim (number) with no citation tag

sentences.sentence: That is the truth of what survives.
We are not going to smooth it over.
